title: Hearing musicians in New Orleans around 1920
summary: Who he did and did not hear in New Orleans, the dating of his stay, and memories of Dodds.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: No. He's in beautiful condition, too. He's in beautiful condition. Did you play with Celestan?
No. You didn't? No. But I heard him play. I heard him play in New Orleans. And you heard Paul Barnes? Oh.

Ridgely? The only one I never heard was P-Roll. It was when I went to Norland for 24 years in Chicago. Oh, yeah. I didn't get to hear. And he had a bunch of nice musicians with him. And I really wanted to hear, but I didn't get a chance.
Which, let's see, that would have been around after the war. See, that would have been probably from 20 to 23, wouldn't it? I'd say. Or 19. 1919 to 22 in there when you were in New Orleans.
Well, no, no, it was, it would have been 20. 20. 20.
Yes. Yeah, because John Dodds hadn't left yet. Johnny Dodds hadn't left there yet.
Boy, I guess it's just as fantastic as they say it was.

I think he can see him settling down in Eli Cabaret as if it was yesterday. He was playing. Boy, he's a young, young man. Swing like mad. I could still, right now, I could see him as if it was yesterday. Just as delicate as he could have played. Well, those guys, he's creative. That's one thing. I never tried to break my head to go and try to do what they were doing. And still, if they were doing, they still are doing. They are creators. They made it possible for all planet players. And it would be sort of foolish for me to go and break my head trying to play like them. Yeah. I love clarinet. I would like to do that style, but I don't have, I don't think the way they think. I can't produce what those guys do.
